![Alopecia Areata: Causes, Treatments, Breakthroughs | 2020 Guide](https://api.dataforseo.com/cdn/i/10181639-2787-0139-0000-492e8952c337:4)
Alopecia areata is `a common autoimmune disease that causes your immune system to mistakenly attack your healthy hair follicles, leading to unpredictable, non-scarring hair loss`.[[1]](https://www.naaf.org/alopecia-areata/)[[2]](https://www.facebook.com/AnneArundelDermatology/posts/alopecia-areata-what-is-it-who-does-it-affect-and-how-do-you-treat-it-chauncey-b/792689586746221/)[[3]](https://www.aad.org/public/diseases/hair-loss/types/alopecia)

### Symptoms & Patterns

- **Patchy Hair Loss:** Typically begins with sudden, smooth, round or oval bald spots on the scalp, beard, eyebrows, or eyelashes.[[1]](https://www.niams.nih.gov/health-topics/alopecia-areata)[[2]](https://www.aad.org/public/diseases/hair-loss/types/alopecia)[[3]](https://ishrs.org/alopecia-areata/)
- **Exclamation Point Hairs:** Short, broken hairs that are narrower at the base than at the tip often appear around the edges of a bare patch.[[1]](https://www.niams.nih.gov/health-topics/alopecia-areata)
- **Nail Changes:** Fingernails or toenails may develop small dents, pits (cupuliform depressions), or a rough, sandpaper-like texture.[[1]](https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/diseases/12423-alopecia-areata)[[2]](https://emedicine.medscape.com/article/1069931-overview)
- **Clinical Variants:** 
	- *Patchy alopecia areata:* One or more coin-sized bald spots.
	- *Ophiasis:* Hair loss in a band along the sides and lower back of the scalp.
	- *Alopecia totalis:* Complete loss of hair on the scalp.
	- *Alopecia universalis:* Total loss of hair across the entire body.[[1]](https://emedicine.medscape.com/article/1069931-overview)[[2]](https://www.naaf.org/navigation-toolkit/understanding-alopecia-areata/)

### Causes & Risk Factors

- **Autoimmune Response:** White blood cells (T-cells) swarm the hair root, causing inflammation and halting growth while breaking the follicle's normal "immune privilege".[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alopecia_areata)[[2]](https://www.facebook.com/AnneArundelDermatology/posts/alopecia-areata-what-is-it-who-does-it-affect-and-how-do-you-treat-it-chauncey-b/792689586746221/)
- **Genetics & Triggers:** It tends to run in families with a genetic predisposition and can be triggered by severe stress, illness, or environmental factors.[[1]](https://ishrs.org/alopecia-areata/)[[2]](https://www.facebook.com/AnneArundelDermatology/posts/alopecia-areata-what-is-it-who-does-it-affect-and-how-do-you-treat-it-chauncey-b/792689586746221/)
- **Associated Conditions:** Frequently linked with other autoimmune or inflammatory issues such as thyroid disease, vitiligo, or atopic dermatitis.[[1]](https://emedicine.medscape.com/article/1069931-overview)

### Prognosis & Treatment

- **Non-Scarring Nature:** Because the hair roots are not permanently destroyed, hair can potentially regrow on its own, though cycles of loss and regrowth are common. Initial regrowth may come back fine and white or blonde before returning to its normal color.[[1]](https://www.aad.org/public/diseases/hair-loss/types/alopecia)[[2]](https://www.bad.org.uk/pils/alopecia-areata)
- **Treatment Options:** While there is no universal cure, dermatologists manage the condition using topical or intralesional (injected) corticosteroids, minoxidil, anthralin, or systemic Janus kinase (JAK) inhibitors. For detailed guidance or patient resources, visit the [National Alopecia Areata Foundation](https://www.naaf.org/).[[1]](https://www.facebook.com/AnneArundelDermatology/posts/alopecia-areata-what-is-it-who-does-it-affect-and-how-do-you-treat-it-chauncey-b/792689586746221/)[[2]](https://emedicine.medscape.com/article/1069931-overview)[[3]](https://www.aad.org/public/diseases/hair-loss/types/alopecia)[[4]](https://www.naaf.org/alopecia-areata/)

If you or someone you know is dealing with this, let me know:

- **Where** the hair loss is located (scalp, beard, body)
- **How long** the patches have been present

I can share more specific details on what to expect or how specialists approach treatment.
